Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen Brisbane’s median price has fallen about $8,000 since May, bringing an end to a historic 40-month incline. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Housing House prices slide across Australia as Middle East conflict and tax changes begin to bite Cotality data shows a drop in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, as nation’s median home price falls about $19,000 below its March peak Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google House prices have fallen in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth as the market downturn spreads across Australia. New Cotality data, released on Monday, showed prices have fallen across most of the nation since May. Brisbane’s median price has fallen about $8,000 since May, to equal its March level of $1.1m. The city’s dwelling prices had increased for an historic 40 consecutive months, since February 2023, until they fell in June. Fines, indefinite motel stays and uncertainty: how a homeless camp exposed regional Australia’s housing crisis Read more Adelaide and Perth median home prices have each fallen about $4,000 below their record highs set in May, at $944,000 and $1.03m respectively. In June, regional Australia’s home values fell overall for the first time since January 2023. Regional home values fell or stayed flat in every state in July. Nationally, the median home price is now $928,000 – about $19,000 below its March peak. Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra median prices have respectively fallen $69,000, $39,000 and $22,000 since February. Prices in Sydney and Melbourne are still higher than they were in January 2025 and in Canberra are above where they were in September 2025. Prices are still higher than January 2025 The Reserve Bank has reported fewer than 1% of borrowers have fallen into negative equity, with home values worth less than their loans, while an even smaller share are unable to make repayments. The housing market has slowed since February, when the Reserve Bank of Australia began to hike interest rates and the US war on Iran broke out. Housing demand has fallen further since the May federal budget trimmed property investors’ tax concessions. Capital gains tax changes are already having an impact on wealth inequality – and vested interests are running scared | Greg Jericho Read more NAB on Thursday reported a 15% fall in home loan applications from the first three months of 2026 to the three months to June. Westpac, Equifax and Loan Market have independently reported falling mortgage demand. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, speaking at an Anika Foundation lunch on Wednesday, said she was surprised by the slump in house prices and housing demand since May. Bullock said interest rates were only “a bit” restrictive, attributing the slump to falling buyer demand. “I expect that things will settle down,” Bullock said. “People will get used to the new rules. Hopefully the conflict overseas will die down, and they’ll get a bit more confidence. Prices might lower a bit. People might feel more confident to come back into the market.” Buyers and sellers are already showing signs of adjustment, with auction clearance rates edging up from from their June low of 47.4% to reach 53.6% at the weekend, according to Cotality’s preliminary data. The property research company reported the number of new listings had declined over July as sellers held off going to market to wait out weak conditions. The RBA is not expected to raise interest rates when its board next meets on 11 August. Estonian Defence Minister resigned over €70M ammo deal. Ammo supplier failed to deliver quality shells for Ukraine. Estonia seeks to recover funds from disputed contract. Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur has resigned following a controversy over a €70 million ammunition procurement meant to support Ukraine, after a government supplier failed to deliver the expected artillery shells on schedule. Pevkur, who has headed Estonia’s defence ministry since 2022, said he was stepping down to accept political responsibility for shortcomings in the defence sector, even as he maintained that he was not personally involved in negotiating individual contracts. “Estonian security is not a one-man project. It is our joint responsibility. That is why I must take political responsibility for the entire defence field today,” Pevkur said in a social media post. The procurement involved Datasel SRL, an Italy-based company acquired by India’s Neco Defence Munitions in 2024. Estonia’s Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK) entered into several contracts with the company to secure artillery ammunition for Ukraine, which was facing shortages of shells during its war with Russia. The deal was financed through the European Union’s European Peace Facility, with Estonia making substantial advance payments. According to Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR and reports by Eesti Ekspress and Postimees , the payments eventually totalled about €70 million. Estonia began contracting Datasel in August 2024, initially paying roughly €15 million upfront. Another agreement followed in October, with additional contracts subsequently taking the advance payments to around €70 million by the end of the year, according to the reports. The ammunition was supposed to be supplied within months. Deliveries were, however, repeatedly delayed amid reported production difficulties. When ammunition was eventually received in 2025, it did not meet the required quality standards, Eesti Ekspress reported. Datasel had no previous record of producing or selling artillery shells and that the ammunition received was not ultimately sent to Ukraine, it has been further learnt from a report by The Telegraph . Following this, RKIK terminated the contracts and sought the return of the advance payments. Estonia has taken the dispute to international arbitration as it attempts to recover the money. The supplier, however, has rejected Estonia's account of the matter. Datasel has argued that it delivered a substantial quantity of munitions and disputed the claims that quality problems justified termination of the contracts. According to Eesti Ekspress , the company said it had supplied goods and submitted invoices worth approximately €58 million. Datasel also confirmed receiving around €59 million in advance payments. “Datasel is the party that has suffered losses in connection with these supply contracts,” the company said through its lawyer, according to the newspaper. It further claimed that the reasons cited by Estonia for terminating the agreements were “contradictory and illogical”. Datasel acknowledged delays but disputed claims that the ammunition supplied was unusable. The company said it was prepared to complete the contracts if RKIK fulfilled its own obligations. The dispute has now become a legal battle, with Estonia seeking to recover the funds and Datasel challenging the termination of its contracts. Elmar Vaher, director general of RKIK, said the contract should not have been awarded to the company in the first place. “In my opinion, we should not have signed a contract with them,” Vaher told Eesti Ekspress . He compared the decision to hiring an inexperienced builder. “If I start building a house and hire a company that has never built houses before, there is a doubt that the house will not be finished,” Vaher said. Pevkur's resignation came as Estonia's National Audit Office scrutinised the country's defence spending and procurement practices. An audit released on August 28 identified problems relating to the management of defence funds and the accounting of military assets, according to ERR . The watchdog warned that Estonia could be forced to bear the €70 million cost from its own budget if the money cannot be recovered from the disputed procurement. The matter has also attracted the attention of the European Commission because the ammunition purchase was financed with EU money. Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said the bloc had safeguards and recovery mechanisms intended to protect EU funds. Pevkur defended the existing division of responsibilities, arguing that ministers do not personally conduct individual procurement negotiations. “The defence minister does not conduct contract negotiations; the defence minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defence minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine,” he said, according to ERR. He also said he had not read the contracts, pointing out that detailed procurement work was handled by RKIK. The minister faced further scrutiny in parliament on Wednesday, where lawmakers questioned him about the procurement controversy. Pevkur described the matter as an “ordinary contract dispute”, while stressing the exceptional pressure on European countries to secure ammunition for Ukraine during a period of global shortages. Estonia's defence procurement agency has previously promoted itself as a fast-moving buyer capable of helping other European countries secure weapons for Ukraine. Pevkur said the agency had executed roughly €400 million in contracts on behalf of international donors. Despite his resignation, Pevkur maintained that Estonia had made the right strategic choices to strengthen its security. “Estonia is better protected than ever before,” he wrote. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Baby Bigfoot impersonator Soren Sadr, 5, runs around the Running Springs farmers market on 11 October 2025, during the first annual Bigfoot Festival. Photograph: MediaNews Group/The San Bernardino Sun/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Baby Bigfoot impersonator Soren Sadr, 5, runs around the Running Springs farmers market on 11 October 2025, during the first annual Bigfoot Festival. Photograph: MediaNews Group/The San Bernardino Sun/Getty Images US news Bigfoot enthusiasts hope government’s US sightings files are ‘just the beginning’ of proving the creature real The Forest Service’s work will ‘help normalize’ talk happening ‘for decades’, says ‘wood ape’ conservancy director Adam Gabbatt Fri 27 Nov 2026 08.00 EST Last modified on Fri 27 Nov 2026 08.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When the Forest Service, one of the US government’s less sexy departments, quietly posted three documents to its website in mid-October, it was probably hoping to avoid a fuss. It didn’t succeed. The files were about Bigfoot, after all, and their publication sparked interest from around the globe, with Bigfoot enthusiasts hopeful that this could be a key step step in the road to proving the creature is real. US releases files on suspected Bigfoot sightings in Montana and Oregon Read more “It’s going to help normalize the conversation that the people in this community have been having for decades,” said Tami Grimes. She’s a director at the North American Wood Ape Conservancy (Nawac), which investigates sightings of Bigfoot (the organization prefers the term ‘wood ape’, as it is less mythical-sounding). Nawac collects reports and, if Bigfoot encounters are deemed legitimate, sends out volunteers to gather, or attempt to gather, evidence. “The release of these papers shows that there have been government reports done to document it. It shows that there was enough to the incidents that the Forest Service took the incidents seriously.” Grimes, 59, has reason to be invested. She said she has seen Bigfoot several times – the first when she was four-years-old. Her family lived close to Green Swamp, in central Florida, and Grimes recalls looking out of the bedroom one night and seeing a bipedal creature, covered in dark brown-to-back colored hair, staring back at her. It was 7ft tall, and powerfully built. “The best way to describe the physique is that it was like Lou Ferrigno,” Grimes said, referring to the bodybuilder-turned-actor who was crowned Mr Universe in 1974 and later played the Hulk in the CBS TV show The Incredible Hulk. “It was broad across the shoulders, incredibly muscular,” she said. The creature, which Grimes believes was a Bigfoot, was not impeded by its bulky frame. It ran off at a “rapid speed”, Grimes recalls. She had nightmares for 25 years after the event. She then had another run-in with a Bigfoot in December 2003, when she and a friend went looking for one in a swamp in Florida. She saw a figure standing in the woods, swaying from side to side. It turned to look at her, Grimes said, then it tried and failed to hide behind a pine tree: “Its face and its backside was still sticking out from behind the tree,” before running off into the woods. Grimes had been watching the figure through a thermal camera, but unfortunately she had only recently purchased the camera and did not know how to press record, so no footage was captured. Bigfoot, or Sasquatch, has captured American imaginations for decades. Believers say the creature inhabits forests in the US and Canada, being particularly common in the Pacific north-west. Commonly described as tall, strong-looking and foul-smelling, there have been thousands of reports of sightings submitted to amateur Bigfoot tracking organizations like Nawac and the Bigfoot field researchers organization. View image in fullscreen Bill Willard, is searching for evidence of a Sasquatch or Bigfoot creature, spotted by, among others, his two sons in Spottsylania county, Virginia, on 19 May 2010. Photograph: Bill O’Leary/The Washington Post/Getty Images Yet Bigfoot is considered by many to be a myth, its alleged existence attributable to folk tales and whimsy, and governmental discussion of it is rare. The White House, the US Department of Defense and the US Department of the Interior all declined to comment on Bigfoot to the Guardian. The Forest Service did reply. In a statement, a spokesman said: “Stories of Bigfoot, Sasquatch, and other legendary beings have long been part of the cultural fabric of many regions, reflecting a rich tradition of folklore, oral history, and storytelling that surrounds our public lands. While the Forest Service does not endorse or make any claims regarding the existence of such creatures, we appreciate the public’s enthusiasm for exploring and learning about our public lands.” Other sources were more forthright. A chatbot on the National Park Service website said there “is no scientific evidence that Bigfoot exists as a real animal”, while Encyclopedia Britannica said “most scientists do not recognize the creature’s existence”. Bigfoot does not feature in the National Wildlife Federation’s database of fauna found in the US. Sasquatch ‘sightings’ reignite fervour and scepticism about ape-like beast Read more The amount of Bigfoot hoaxes likely hasn’t helped boost its credibility. In one case, two men said they found a Bigfoot body, but when they handed it over to researchers it turned out to be a rubber gorilla suit. A 2014 study of 30 hair samples alleged to be yeti or Bigfoot found that all the hair was from extant species, including a black bear, a cow and a human. Still, there was plenty of excitement when the forestry service quietly released those Bigfoot-related documents, even if the content was a little underwhelming. One of the files was merely a copy of a newspaper article, which reported that mysterious tracks had been discovered in Montana. Another was a 1980 essay written by someone called Leo Kinney , in which Kinney wrote that he and three others had encountered something in the woods: a creature “that walked on its hind legs that altho [sic] there wasn’t actual sightings, tracks, a strong odor and a gruntling sound were observed”. The file that received the most attention was probably a report which had been commissioned by the US Department of Agriculture. In the report, Rodney Johnson, a wildlife biologist, said the USDA had asked him to accompany a group in the Umatilla national forest, in Portland, to investigate a reported finding of Bigfoot tracks – suggesting that at least someone at the department thought Bigfoot worthy of further study. Johnson made plaster casts of four different foot or paw prints at two locations in the forest. He examined them, but found that the tracks “were made by something other than a 300 pound plus two-footed being” – aka, not Bigfoot. Johnson listed eight reasons for his conclusion, finding that the tracks did not extend deeply into the mud, that the stride length did not change even when they tracked uphill, that “forest litter”, like leaves, had been brushed aside prior to making the track, and that the tracks came to an abrupt end in the forest. Some Bigfoot theories, however, account for that last point. “It sounds more and more like alien or extraterrestrial than it does animal,” said Ronny LeBlanc, who starred in the Travel Channel show Expedition Bigfoot, which saw him and other experts search for Bigfoot at various locations. LeBlanc believes Bigfoot, or the creature known as Bigfoot, may be inter-dimensional or may use telepathy – or both – to evade capture. “We’re hearing about UFOs coming in and out of the water. We’re hearing about underwater bases and all this stuff,” LeBlanc said, echoing claims made by UFO-curious Republican congressman Tim Burchett. Burchett, who has been a lead figure in demanding the government release information pertaining to UFOs, said last year that an admiral had told him about large unidentified craft “moving at hundreds of miles an hour underwater”. “So for me, it’s not that far of a stretch that you have something running around in the forest,” LeBlanc said. View image in fullscreen ‘Commonly described as tall, strong-looking and foul-smelling, there have been thousands of reports of sightings submitted to amateur Bigfoot tracking organizations like Nawac and the Bigfoot field researchers organization.’ Photograph: Nicole Weaver/Alamy He has had his own Bigfoot experiences. He said he and another man once encountered an “orange orb” in a forest, which “split into two eyes” before taking on the shape of an 8ft tall Bigfoot. “We were with a clairvoyant medium, so I don’t know if that had something to do with it,” LeBlanc said. He compared the relatively low lack of sightings of Bigfoot to the case of air force pilots who were reluctant to tell their commanding officers that they had seen UFOs. Several finally came forward and shared their experiences with the 60 Minutes news show in 2021, sparking an increased interest in a taboo subject, and prompting several congressional hearings. “In that same vein, you have people [asking]: “How come hunters don’t see [Bigfoot]? or ‘How come loggers don’t see them?’ “They do. They’re just not talking about it,” he said. “Forestry workers are finding nests in tracks and having sightings, and they’re afraid to kind of pass it up the chain.” LeBlanc said the Forest Service releasing the three reports could be “just the beginning” in terms of encouraging more conversation and disclosure. “They’re going to start releasing more of these types of things, probably coming right from the US department of agriculture,” he said. “And I think some of the UFO files that are going to get dropped: they’re going to contain some Bigfoot stuff.” Should a Bigfoot be discovered, it probably wouldn’t meet a happy fate. It’s easy to imagine it becoming a target for hunters or others who might wish it ill, and even Bigfoot friendly organizations pose a threat. Asked what it would take to definitively prove Bigfoot’s existence, Tami Grimes, from Nawac, said it would essentially require the group killing one then hauling it off to some scientists for inspection. “That is part of our mission. It’s uncomfortable, but it is what science demands,” Grimes said. She said Nawac has a small cadre of volunteer hunters who are prepared to shoot dead a Bigfoot, which Grimes said would likely be necessary, because capturing a live Bigfoot would be too difficult. Whether mammal, or alien, or Lou Ferrigno in an elaborate costume, Bigfoot is probably better off not being found.
